explanation: Fires on the token 'de'/'De'/'DE' (usually space-prefixed) used as a word-initial piece, whether a prefix (de-centralized, deoxy-, depleting, debris, devious) or a name particle (de Tocqueville, de Kooning, De Hra Dun). It is weaker for related d-initial pieces like 'dec', 'dem', 'di', 'dela' and near zero for other tokens.

Fires on a conjunction or separator ('or', 'and', a comma) and on the first item of a coordinated pair or list, especially in numeric ranges like '3 or 4', '50 years or longer', '2.5:1 or greater'. Strongest on 'or' right after a number. Moderate on 'and'/commas joining noun phrases and on items inside number lists.

Fires on a word fragment early in a word, often the first subword piece of a rare, foreign or technical word (t|atuado, circ|ov|irus, D|rosophila, d|engue, M|ā|ori, hant|av|iruses), and on some tokens in non-English (Spanish, French, German) text. No consistent meaning; it seems to track mid-word or unusual-tokenization positions rather than a concept.

Fires in narrative prose and fiction on tokens that start a new sentence or clause, or come right after one: a paragraph-initial 'The', a closing quote plus comma, a subject followed by an action verb ('Austin stood', 'she reached', 'Bridich sat'). It responds to story or quote structure rather than to specific words, and is weak in expository text.

Fires on a single digit token inside a long digit string, such as an ID, docket number, phone number, timestamp, DOI, page number or year (e.g. the inner digits of 'CP-02-CR-0005355', '01923 676601'). Strongest in long serial or ID-like numbers. Moderate on digits in dates and years. Near zero on non-numeric tokens.

Mixed. It fires on scaffold tokens in formulaic boilerplate (abstract openers like 'The purpose of this article is', 'Introduction', degree mentions like 'B.A.'/'degree', 'covered by' in license text) and also on unrelated tokens such as word-completion pieces (chimpan|zee, mam|moth) and code identifiers. No single clear trigger.

Fires on a wide, unrelated mix of tokens: SVG path letters, Devanagari pieces, code indentation and closing braces, math expression numbers, ordinary nouns ('message', 'ceramic', 'conditions'). No shared feature is visible.

Fires in source code on the name of a function, method or constructor at the point where it is declared: the identifier right after 'def', 'function', 'public' or a type, or after the class name in a constructor ('public Phonebook()', 'def fit(', 'function create()'), plus the parentheses that follow. It is weaker on other identifiers and near zero in prose.

Fires mostly on the subword pieces of proper names and foreign-language words (Finnish, French, Portuguese), e.g. K|ait|lyn, El|way, T|yr|anny, t|iet|ysti, and also on some common verbs in foreign or English text ('a', 'has', 'nearly'). The trigger looks like non-English or name tokenization, but the set is loosely bound.

Fires on subword pieces inside biomedical and scientific technical terms (radios|urgery, DB|S, radi|ol|abeled, strept|oc|occi, nivolum|ab, methad|one, 'cosmic microwave'), and moderately on path strings in require('../') code. It mainly tracks technical or medical jargon, with a few unrelated hits.

Fires on a title or role word that comes right before a person's name: the period after 'Rev'/'Gov'/'Rep', or the end of 'Rabbi', 'Colonel', 'Cardinal', 'Datuk', 'District Judge'. It is weaker on job titles in other positions ('governor of', 'chairman', 'CEO'). Strongest on political, religious and judicial honorifics.

Fires on the first one or two subword pieces at the start of a word that is split into several tokens, often a name or less common word (Pierre Fr|ondaie, Br|ötzmann, de|bridement, BY|D, Con|ductor, dr|ifter). It is the word-onset piece of a multi-token word in any language. Whole common words give little activation.

Fires on the honorific 'Mr'/'MR'/'Ms' or the period after it, just before a surname (e.g. 'Mr Goodwill', 'Mr. Bush'), especially in news text. It is weaker on other titles like Dr, Capt, Secretary, Lord and Baroness.

Fires on a heterogeneous set of tokens: 'time' in 'time stamp', 'To:' in email headers, 'methanol' pieces, '@author', 'Super Bowl', biomedical terms, 'the' in 'claims the benefit'. No common pattern stands out.

Fires on function words inside quantifier or partitive and fixed phrases: 'of' after most/any/all/some ('most of them'), 'no' in 'by no means'/'of no fault'/'in no way', and also 'am' in 'I am' or 'What am I'. It mainly tracks partitive 'of' and idiomatic 'no', with scattered other hits.

Fires in object-oriented source code on class or interface declaration structure: protocol and interface names (NSCopying, UIViewControllerAnimated), '__construct', '@interface', 'namespace', '@property', and the indentation that starts a member line inside a class body. It is weak outside code.

Fires most strongly on 'other(s)' in the phrase 'among other things'/'among others'. It also fires on unrelated tokens: the '{' in LaTeX '\begin{array}', 'Code' in 'XCode', and comment markers '#'/'//' that start a line after a license header.

Fires on the digit '6' inside a number, especially the decade or century digit of a year ('1967', '1631', '1861') and in postal codes, ports and other numbers. It is weaker on '60'/'six' and near zero on other digits.

Fires mostly on line breaks and line-start tokens in structured config or metadata files (package.toml, JSON, YAML front matter, pom.xml, .pro files), plus the subword 'prop'/'Pro' starting words like proposta, Proposed, Prophecy and Providence. It mixes a structured-file boundary feature with a 'prop' token feature.

Fires on 'to' in 'how to' or 'way to' after expressions of not knowing ('I don't know how to fix', 'not sure how to'), mostly in Q&A or help-seeking text. It also fires on the subword 'az' (Waziristan, Spazigaster) and sometimes on 'of'/'Berlin' in fixed phrases.

Fires on a non-initial subword piece of an all-caps word or name (BIRMING|HAM, G|IL|BERT, SN|OW, G|LEN|DALE, LE|ADER), and on caps headline openers ('MOST', 'JUST', 'HIGH'). It responds to the inside of uppercase text in general.
